lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: The Infinite Song. One song, since the beginning of time. You're just in time.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: This is Ambrose Long, on The Infinite Song.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Still going.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: The Infinite Song, one oh five point four. Don't worry about the start. Nobody heard the start.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: You're listening to The Infinite Song. This is the bit you like.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Good morning. This is The Morning Verse. The song carried on while you slept. Here's where we've got to.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: While you were asleep: twelve verses, one key change, attempted, and a very long bit about a lighthouse.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: The lighthouse is fine. The boat is back. Good morning.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: This is Chorus Watch. Ears open, everyone. Today could be the day.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: It won't be. But it could.

lines.speaker: A Listener in the Overlap
lines.text: Ambrose, I'm sure I heard the chorus. In the shower.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: That's a very common sighting. It's nearly always the shower. We've logged it. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: A report from the Overlap. At three o'clock this afternoon, the bass player hummed something chorus-shaped.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: We've checked the tape. It was a yawn. We remain hopeful.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: The Night Verses. I'll keep count.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: You rest.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Verse four million, one hundred and twelve. Line six. The boat again.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: It's a good boat. It's been a good boat for thousands of years.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: To the operator on the relay ship. If you're keeping a log, put down verse four million, one hundred and twelve. Roughly.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Someone in the future will thank you. Or argue. Either way, it's company.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: The lines are open. You're on The Infinite Song. Which verse are you on?

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Let's go to the phones. Quietly, now, so we don't lose the beat. Hello, you're on the air.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Hello, caller. Keep your voice down. We're in a delicate bit.

lines.speaker: Marek, Catching Up
lines.text: Hi, Ambrose. I'm on verse four million and ninety. I fell asleep around verse eighty, and I'm catching up.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Not to worry. The song waits for no one, but it does repeat itself a bit. You'll have caught up by Thursday.

lines.speaker: Gwendolyn, Third Generation
lines.text: My grandmother's grandmother's grandmother heard verse one. She always said it was about a boat.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: A lot of people's grandmothers say that. The archive is unclear. There's definitely a boat by verse eleven. Before that, it's mostly someone tuning up.

lines.speaker: A Caller Waiting for the Chorus
lines.text: Is the chorus coming back? I've been told there's a chorus.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: There is a chorus. It was last heard in verse nine hundred thousand and six. Experts believe it's due.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Experts have believed that for some time.

lines.speaker: A Drummer in a Young Band
lines.text: My band wants to cover it. How long have we got?

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: How long have any of us got, really? Start at the first verse. Let us know how you get on.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Or your grandchildren can.

lines.speaker: Teodor, Relay Four
lines.text: Can anyone hear me? This is Teodor. Relay Four.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: We can hear you, Teodor. Which verse are you on?

lines.speaker: Teodor, Relay Four
lines.text: Two thousand and six. The signal is very slow out here.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Then you've a lovely few million ahead of you, Teodor. Don't skip anything.

lines.speaker: Bev
lines.text: Hello, love. Is this the request line?

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: It is, Bev. Though we only have the one song.

lines.speaker: Bev
lines.text: Oh, that's all right. Could you play it?

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: We're playing it now, Bev.

lines.speaker: Bev
lines.text: Lovely. I'll wait for my bit.

lines.speaker: Lionel, Also Counting
lines.text: Ambrose, I think you've miscounted. I make it verse four million, one hundred and eleven.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Do you. Well. I've been counting since I was six.

lines.speaker: Lionel, Also Counting
lines.text: So have I.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Let's call it a hundred and eleven and a half, Lionel.

lines.speaker: Toby, Aged Nine
lines.text: Mister Long, what happens at the end?

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Nobody knows, Toby. Some people think it never ends. Some think it ends and starts again.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: I think it ends when the last person stops listening. So I try never to stop.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Thank you for calling. Back to the song. It never left.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Lovely. Let's rejoin the verse. They're on the bit about the boat again.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Thanks for ringing in. Mind the beat on your way out.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Verse count update. We are now on verse four million, one hundred and twelve.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Or thirteen. I blinked.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: A verse has just finished, and another has begun. Very like the last one, but with a good deal more about a goat.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: I don't know where the goat has come from. I'm sure it'll explain itself.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: For anyone just joining us, this is verse four million, one hundred and fourteen. Welcome.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: You haven't missed much. Well. You've missed nearly all of it. But not much.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: News from the stage. Old Wendeline, on drums, has kept the beat with her left hand since the Iron Age. Tonight she has switched to her right.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: The beat is exactly the same. We all felt it, though.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: A little history. The song began before the first morning. Nobody wrote it down, because nobody had invented writing.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Then somebody did invent writing, and the first thing they wrote was: how long is this going on for?

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: The band have asked me to mention their beards. The beards are now out of the stage door and halfway down the high street.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: The post office has asked us to mention it too. Please step over them gently. They're very old.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Verse four million, one hundred and thirteen is the spooky one. It comes round at this time every year. Nobody knows how.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: It's the one with the lantern, and a door that isn't there. The band always play it a little quieter.

lines.speaker: A Caller With Good Ears
lines.text: Ambrose, I think there's a ghost on the backing vocals.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: That'll be Ephraim. He was the original backing singer. He's been gone four thousand years.

lines.speaker: A Caller With Good Ears
lines.text: Oh.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: He's never missed a verse. Happy Halloween, Ephraim.

lines.speaker: Ephraim, Backing Vocals
lines.text: Happy Halloween, Ambrose.

lines.speaker: A Caller With Good Ears
lines.text: ...I'm going to go and sit with the lights on.

lines.speaker: Ambrose Long
lines.text: Very sensible. Mind the beat.
